A practical guide to wedding gratuities: who is tipped, how service charges change the answer, and who hands out the envelopes.
Wedding Vendor Tipping Guide
Check the contract before budgeting tips. A service charge may already cover gratuities, and some business owners prefer not to be tipped at all.
First check
Read the contract for service charge, gratuity and 'all inclusive'
Common
Hair, makeup, drivers, delivery staff and catering teams
Owners
A studio owner may decline a tip; an employee usually will not
Logistics
Labelled envelopes, one trusted person, end of the night

Separate three things that are often confused: a mandatory service charge added by the venue, a discretionary gratuity for the service team, and a thank-you to a creative vendor. Only the last two are decisions you make. Ask each vendor whether their staff are pooled or individual, and whether a cash gratuity is customary for them.

In the US tipping is widely expected for service staff and often for hair, makeup and transport; a 15–25% service charge on catering may or may not reach the staff, so ask. In the UK and much of Europe service is usually included and a tip is a genuine optional thank-you rather than an expectation. In Japan and several other countries tipping can be awkward or refused; a written thank-you or a small gift is safer.

Do not tip on the total bill when a large part is venue hire or equipment rental. Do not hand out cash during the event — appoint one person with labelled envelopes and a checklist. And do not skip the review: for many small vendors a detailed public review is worth more than the cash.
Is a service charge the same as a tip?
Not necessarily. A service charge is a contract line that may cover operations rather than staff gratuities. Ask the venue directly how it is distributed.
Should we tip the photographer?
If they are an employee or a second shooter, a thank-you is common; if they own the studio, many decline. There is no fixed rule.
When do we hand out tips?
At the end of the night, through one designated person with labelled envelopes. Doing it mid-event leads to missed people and awkward handoffs.
